etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English nothyng, noon thing, non thing, na þing, nan thing, nan þing, from Old English nāþing, nān þing (“nothing”, literally “not any thing”), equivalent to no +‎ thing. Compare Old English nāwiht (“nothing”, literally “no thing”), Swedish ingenting (“nothing”, literally “not any thing, no thing”).

quote.text: the players see little or nothing of their cards at first starting

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XIX, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Nothing was too small to receive attention, if a supervising eye could suggest improvements likely to conduce to the common welfare. Mr. Gordon Burnage, for instance, personally visited dust-bins and back premises, accompanied by a sort of village bailiff, going his round like a commanding officer doing billets.

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Peter Wilby, “Finland spreads word on schools”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 30:
quote.text: Imagine a country where children do nothing but play until they start compulsory schooling at age seven. Then, without exception, they attend comprehensives until the age of 16. Charging school fees is illegal, and so is sorting pupils into ability groups by streaming or setting.

definitions.definition: An absence of anything, including empty space, brightness, darkness, matter, or a vacuum.
Something trifling, or of no consequence or importance.

quote.citation: 1651–1653, Jer[emy] Taylor, ΕΝΙΑΥΤΟΣ [Eniautos]. A Course of Sermons for All the Sundays of the Year. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  Richard Royston […], published 1655, →OCLC:
quote.text: Sermons are not like curious inquiries after new nothings, but pursuances of old truths.

definitions.definition: A trivial remark especially in the term sweet nothings.
(archaic) Not at all; in no way.

quote.text: The answer was an impatient one—but, nothing daunted, he continued.

quote.citation: 1662, Thomas Salusbury, Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two World Systems:
quote.text: The Motion from London to Syria is as much as nothing; and nothing altereth the relation which is between them.
